page: Amazon Web Services m8id.large is a general-purpose instance powered by a dedicated Intel Xeon 6975P-C processor. It features 2 vCPUs mapped to a single physical core with 2 threads per core, operating at a clock speed of 3.9 GHz. The instance is equipped with 8.0 GB of DDR5 memory running at 7 GHz, providing 4.0 GB of RAM per core. Local storage is bundled as a 118 GB NVMe SSD instance store volume, and the network interface provides a baseline bandwidth of 1 Gbps. The underlying virtualization is managed by the AWS Nitro hypervisor.

Benchmark data reveals a stark contrast between single-core and multi-core performance. The instance demonstrates strong single-core capabilities, scoring in the top 25% for Geekbench single-core, single-threaded gzip compression, single-threaded bzip3 decompression, and Geekbench text processing. However, because it relies on a single physical core, multi-core performance is constrained, with stress-ng multi-core performance falling into the bottom 10% and Geekbench multi-core scoring in the bottom 25%. Memory performance is also a limiting factor, as large-block read-only memory bandwidth is poor, falling in the bottom 10%, and Passmark memory scores are weak.

From a qualitative cost-efficiency perspective, the m8id.large offers a modern DDR5 memory architecture and high-speed local NVMe storage, but its low core count and weak multi-threaded scaling limit its utility for dense parallel processing. It is best suited for workloads that rely heavily on single-threaded performance, such as text processing, basic file compression, and lightweight general-purpose applications. It is less optimal for database operations, software compilation, or multi-threaded web serving, where benchmarks indicate weak performance.
description: Amazon Web Services m8id.large is a general-purpose instance utilizing the AWS Nitro hypervisor and an x86_64 Intel Xeon 6975P-C processor. It features 2 vCPUs across 1 physical core, 8.0 GB of DDR5 memory, and a 118 GB local NVMe SSD instance store. While single-core benchmarks are strong, with top 25% performance in Geekbench single-core, text processing, and single-threaded gzip compression, the instance faces significant multi-core limitations. Stress-ng multi-core performance falls in the bottom 10%, and memory bandwidth for large blocks is similarly poor. Consequently, this instance provides a qualitative balance of high-speed local storage and DDR5 memory for single-threaded tasks, but is less efficient for parallel processing. It is best suited for lightweight general-purpose workloads, text processing, and single-threaded utility scripts, rather than intensive database operations or multi-threaded applications.
